REWARD—an open-source framework for identifying the unknown benefits of existing medications to inform drug discovery, development, and repurposing

Methods/software framework paper describing large-scale real-world evidence screening for potential beneficial drug–outcome associations using OMOP-standardized data, self-controlled cohort screening, targeted active-comparator new-user analyses, empirical calibration, and cross-database synthesis.

Scope warning. This paper describes and motivates a hypothesis-generation/refinement framework. It does not establish that any REWARD-identified drug–outcome association is a clinically effective new indication, and the authors explicitly position SCC results as signals requiring more tailored follow-up.

One-page synthesis

Core thesis. REWARD operationalizes a very large “all-by-all” search over medications and clinical outcomes in OMOP-mapped real-world data. Its scalable self-controlled cohort (SCC) screen is intended to generate candidate protective associations; prioritized pairs can then receive higher-rigor active comparator new-user (ACNU) analysis with large-scale propensity scores. Negative-control empirical calibration, cross-database replication, meta-analysis, filtering, and clinical review are layered on top to reduce systematic error and focus follow-up.
Why it mattersThe framework converts claims-scale observational data from a narrow “one exposure, one outcome” paradigm into a reusable discovery system. Its strongest contribution is not a particular repurposing claim but an architecture for systematically generating, calibrating, filtering, and interrogating billions of possible drug–outcome associations.
What is actually demonstratedThe manuscript documents the framework, current implementation, computational scale, dashboard, and prior use cases. It reports 14,466 RxNorm ingredients, 160,955 SNOMED conditions, three outcome variants per condition, six current data sources, a 98-GB SCC result store, and prior analyses in dementia, memantine, and SGLT2-inhibitor use cases.
Highest-value method ideaUse a cheap, broad design for discovery and a more expensive causal design for refinement. SCC exploits within-person comparison and computational efficiency; ACNU adds active comparators and LSPS matching but is reserved for selected exposures because of comparator-selection and compute burden.
Most important cautionScale does not convert observational associations into causal evidence. SCC remains vulnerable to protopathic bias and time-varying confounding; ACNU remains vulnerable to unmeasured confounding. Manual biological plausibility review and pair-specific downstream studies remain essential.
Illustrative value of calibration. Figure 5’s atomoxetine–dementia example shows a pooled uncalibrated relative risk of 0.74 (95% CI 0.62–0.89) becoming a calibrated 0.78 (0.54–1.13; P=.19). That visual makes the authors’ central methodological point concrete: empirical calibration can materially alter whether an apparently protective association remains inferentially persuasive.
What this source should not be used for. It should not be treated as confirmation that the published candidate associations prevent dementia, treat psychiatric disease, or constitute approved/validated repurposing opportunities. The framework is explicitly optimized for hypothesis generation and refinement rather than definitive hypothesis testing.

Section condensation

Background

The authors argue that real-world data are routinely used for focused medication safety/effectiveness questions but remain underused for discovering unknown beneficial associations. REWARD is presented as a way to search broadly across medication–outcome relationships to support three goals: infer disease mechanisms that may inform novel interventions, prioritize additional indications for molecules in development, and identify repurposing opportunities for marketed drugs.

The paper’s stated contribution is the first comprehensive description of REWARD as a complete open-source analytic system, rather than another disease-specific output from the framework. Portability is built around the OMOP common data model so that other groups can implement, validate, and extend the approach in their own mapped databases.

Materials and methods — “all-by-all” framing

REWARD supports two reciprocal questions: for one medication, which outcomes appear less frequent during exposure; or for one outcome, which medications appear protective. Operationally, the framework therefore attempts an “all-by-all” association screen spanning the medication and outcome universes available in OMOP vocabularies.

This scale drives the two-tier design strategy used throughout the paper: a computationally efficient SCC design serves as the broad screening workhorse, while ACNU is applied selectively to prioritized exposures because propensity-score modeling and comparator selection are substantially more expensive.

Defining exposure and outcome cohorts

Drug ingredients are defined with RxNorm (14,466 ingredients) and drug classes with ATC (939 classes at hierarchy level 4). Precomputed drug eras define exposure; first exposure is the index date, exposure follow-up begins one day later, and continues until discontinuation or censoring. The software also permits custom exposure definitions, such as formulation-specific cohorts.

Outcomes use 160,955 SNOMED conditions and are primarily incident outcomes. Each condition can be represented by three variants: one diagnosis; two or more diagnoses; or inpatient diagnosis / repeated diagnoses outside the inpatient setting. Custom outcome cohorts can add complex logic or multi-code definitions.

Causal inference models — design split

The SCC design asks whether events occur less often during drug exposure than during an immediately preceding period in the same individuals. ACNU asks whether outcomes occur less often among new users of the target drug than among new users of a chosen comparator. The paper treats SCC as hypothesis generation and ACNU as higher-rigor hypothesis refinement.

Concordant results across the two designs can strengthen interpretation, but discordance is not automatically failure: the designs answer different causal questions and have different bias structures. The authors explicitly warn that SCC is vulnerable to time-varying confounding and protopathic bias, whereas ACNU still cannot eliminate unmeasured confounding.

Self-controlled cohort (SCC)

Each exposed person contributes an exposed period and an immediately preceding unexposed period of equal duration. Drug exposure extends from initiation until discontinuation/end of observation, with a 30-day permissible refill gap. The index date itself is excluded from both periods because same-day exposure/outcome temporal ordering is usually unavailable in claims data.

For each drug–outcome pair, incidence rates are calculated in the exposed and unexposed periods and combined as an incidence rate ratio (IRR). IRR <1 is interpreted as fewer outcomes during exposure and therefore a potential protective signal; IRR >1 suggests increased risk. The self-controlled structure removes time-invariant between-person confounding but does not address time-varying factors.

Active comparator new-user (ACNU)

ACNU is used “one-by-all,” not all-by-all. Target exposures can be selected because of SCC signals, mechanistic interest, relevance to a molecule in development, or repurposing interest. New users of the target treatment are matched 1:1 to comparator users with large-scale propensity scores that may include tens of thousands of covariates from demographics, diagnoses, medications, procedures, measurements, and utilization.

The propensity model uses L1-regularized (LASSO) regression. Covariate balance is considered acceptable when standardized mean differences are ≤0.10. If propensity-score overlap or post-adjustment balance is inadequate, the pair-specific analysis is terminated in that database. Conditioned Cox models estimate HRs; both calibrated and uncalibrated estimates/95% CIs are generated, but the investigators use calibrated results for inference.

Empirical calibration

Both SCC and ACNU use negative-control outcomes that are not known or hypothesized to be causally related to the exposure/comparator. The study design is run over these controls to estimate the distribution of systematic error. The expected null distribution is centered near an effect estimate of 1.0 with roughly 5% nominally significant at P<.05.

The observed control distribution is then used to calibrate the outcome models. The paper gives an example where a mean negative-control IRR of 0.80 would imply a 20% systematic bias in the protective direction. Figure 5 demonstrates that this step can widen uncertainty and remove nominal statistical significance in an apparently protective association.

Data sources

REWARD is designed for any database mapped to OMOP CDM. The paper names Merative MarketScan Commercial Claims and Encounters, Medicare, and Medicaid; Optum Clinformatics Extended Data Mart; JMDC claims; and HealthVerity Comprehensive Claims as recent sources. When multiple databases are analyzed, the framework meta-analyzes effect estimates across available sources.

The current all-by-all environment described in Results uses five US claims databases and one Japanese claims database. Portability is a design goal, but the empirical examples in this paper remain dominated by administrative claims rather than a broad range of OMOP data modalities.

Filtering criteria and manual review

The typical post-calibration screen keeps estimates with IRR/HR <0.70, P<.05, and evidence meeting the first two criteria in at least two databases. An optional risk filter can remove signals showing marked increased risk (for example, IRR/HR >2.0) in at least one database. Meta-analytic results can also serve as an alternative filter.

Surviving SCC results require manual review, especially to remove protopathic associations where the drug indication itself explains the apparent protective relationship. The authors recommend clinical plausibility assessment, review of preclinical/clinical/case evidence, and grouping of related mechanisms. REWARD is explicitly presented as a narrowing device before pair-specific observational studies, small clinical studies, or triangulation with other evidence sources.

System architecture

The system is organized around a central REWARD database and three functional components: protocol specification, analytics execution, and data exploration/aggregation. Protocol settings flow to the analytic layer; raw results return to the central database; meta-analysis, filtering, queries, visualization, and the R Shiny viewer operate over aggregated non-patient-level outputs.

The implementation is written in R, depends on OHDSI HADES and Java, stores aggregated results in PostgreSQL, and exports intermediate CSV files so reviewers can verify privacy/licensing compliance. The source paper points to public GitHub vignettes for configuration, analytic methods, workflow, and dashboard creation, but those external materials were not independently audited here.

Results — scale of the applied framework

The manuscript reports 14,466 unique drug ingredients and 160,955 SNOMED clinical findings; with three outcome variants per condition, it describes nearly 7 billion potential unique exposure–outcome pairs. Across six data sources, the narrative estimates on the order of 50 billion effect-size models in the theoretical maximum, while actual output is much smaller because many medications or outcomes are too rare.

Figure 4 illustrates a narrower count based directly on 14,466 × 160,955 (~2.33 billion raw drug/condition pairs before the three outcome variants). With >0 patients, 3,138 exposures and 23,437 outcomes yield ~73.5 million viable unique pairs; at ≥100 patients, 2,758 exposures and 22,460 outcomes yield ~61.9 million; at ≥1,000 patients, 2,235 exposures and 19,585 outcomes yield ~43.8 million. The paper does not explicitly reconcile the figure’s ~2.33-billion base with the text’s ~7-billion count, but the difference is consistent with the text counting three outcome variants.

Results — computational burden and dashboard

The authors’ implementation used an Azure VM with 8 vCPUs and 64 GiB memory for orchestration, Azure Databricks serverless SQL (XLarge), and distributed execution auto-scaling to as many as four clusters. The all-by-all SCC result tables totaled 98 GB in the PostgreSQL server. ACNU burden is higher because run time depends heavily on patient count, covariate dimensionality, population heterogeneity, and source-data richness.

The dashboard allows exposure/outcome selection, result-table inspection, database-specific estimates, forest plots, calibrated versus uncalibrated results, and empirical-calibration plots. Filters expose benefit threshold, risk threshold, P-value cut-off, required data sources, and source-specific screening criteria. Figure 5 uses atomoxetine and earliest-event dementia as a worked interface example.

Use cases

The authors identify three intended uses. First, REWARD can generate mechanistic clues for new drug development; cited prior applications include dementia, Parkinson disease, PTSD, and depressive/bipolar disorders. Second, an approved drug with a mechanism similar to a molecule in development can provide RWE that helps prioritize additional indications before the investigational drug is approved.

Third, REWARD can support direct repurposing of marketed drugs, especially in rare diseases or other areas with inadequate therapies. These remain discovery uses: the framework supplies candidates for further study rather than replacing confirmatory observational or interventional evaluation.

Published example 1 — all drugs vs dementia (SCC)

A prior REWARD dementia analysis screened 2,181 medications across four US claims databases containing more than 117 million individuals. Drugs already used for dementia and acute inpatient treatments were excluded. Seventeen medications met the stated filter of IRR ≤0.50 and P<.05 in at least two databases with no database showing significant IRR >2.0.

The 17 medications clustered into catecholamine modulators, anticoagulants, antibiotics/antivirals, anticonvulsants, and miscellaneous drugs. The current paper presents these as hypothesis-generating associations and notes biological plausibility, not as evidence that these classes should be prescribed to prevent dementia.

Published example 2 — memantine vs all outcomes (SCC)

A prior memantine analysis included 312,336 new users across four US claims databases and 20,953 SNOMED outcomes with at least one event. Requiring IRR ≤0.50 and P<.05 in at least two databases, while excluding dementia/memory outcomes already related to the indication, left 60 outcomes.

Those 60 included 28 mental-health outcomes, 24 substance-use outcomes, 4 pain outcomes, 3 gastrointestinal/colon-related outcomes, and 1 demyelinating-disease outcome. Again, these are screening signals, and the source does not claim that memantine is proven effective for those conditions.

Published example 3 — SGLT2 inhibitor vs comparators (ACNU)

An ACNU analysis studied an SGLT2 inhibitor against two comparator diabetes treatments across five real-world databases. Restricting SNOMED outcomes to those with at least 300 events reduced the candidate universe from more than 100,000 outcomes to 1,850.

After empirical calibration, 13 outcomes met the signal threshold of HR ≤0.70 and P≤.05 in at least two databases. Concepts included kidney disease, heart failure, anemia, and vomiting. This example illustrates the more targeted ACNU refinement stage rather than all-by-all deployment.

Discussion

The authors emphasize three differentiators: open-source implementation, OMOP-standardized vocabularies for cross-database portability, and integration of pharmacoepidemiologic methods such as empirical calibration and LSPS. They frame the system as a reusable discovery infrastructure rather than a one-off analysis and argue that open methods improve external validation compared with proprietary approaches.

They also state the central limitation plainly: REWARD is better suited to hypothesis generation/refinement than definitive testing. SCC needs intensive curation for protopathic bias and time-varying confounding; ACNU needs careful comparator selection and large compute. Future versions are expected to add automated comparator selection, more scalable propensity-score approaches, and additional study designs. Observational chance findings, confounding, and information bias remain possible despite calibration, filtering, and clinical review.

Conclusion and transparency

The conclusion argues that OMOP-mapped health systems can use REWARD to generate drug-benefit hypotheses for unmet medical needs and that open-source distribution supports reproducible scientific development. The strongest defensible conclusion is therefore about the feasibility and architecture of large-scale RWE hypothesis generation, not the clinical efficacy of any specific repurposing candidate.

No external funding was reported. All authors are Johnson & Johnson employees and stockholders. The software is reported as publicly accessible, while the underlying example data are governed by data-use agreements and cannot be redistributed by the authors.

Figure 1 — Self-controlled cohort design

Purpose: define the scalable SCC screening unit.
Structure: one patient acts as their own control.
Timeline:
  equal-duration unexposed period immediately before index
  → index date (first observed drug dispensing; excluded from both windows)
  → exposed period beginning the next day and continuing through inferred use
Exposure continuity: dispensing supply can bridge refills with a 30-day gap allowance.
Outcome: first incident outcome can occur in either period.
Effect measure: IRR = exposed incidence rate / unexposed incidence rate.
Interpretation: IRR < 1 = candidate protective association; IRR > 1 = candidate increased risk.
Key limitation: time-varying confounding and protopathic bias remain.

Figure 2 — Active comparator new-user cohort design

Purpose: refine selected hypotheses with a stronger between-treatment comparison.
Target: new users of drug of interest.
Comparator: new users of an active alternative drug.
Adjustment: large-scale propensity score; 1:1 matching; tens of thousands of covariates may enter the model.
Follow-up: inferred duration of treatment until discontinuation/censoring.
Outcome: captured in both matched groups.
Effect measure: conditioned Cox proportional hazards model (HR), with empirical calibration.
Key limitation: comparator choice, compute burden, and residual/unmeasured confounding.

Evaluation and appraisal

Verdict: Read first. Best use: a high-value methods/architecture reference for large-scale observational drug-benefit screening, OMOP-based research infrastructure, and bias-aware hypothesis generation. Do not use for: clinical prescribing decisions or confirmation of repurposed indications.
9/10
RelevanceHighly relevant to pharmacoepidemiology, clinical informatics, RWE infrastructure, and drug-repurposing workflows.
Evidence basis: end-to-end OMOP/HADES system, study designs, calibration, dashboard, implementation details. Limiting factor: it is not direct clinical-efficacy evidence. Would rise: only if the task specifically centers on population-level RWE discovery. Would fall: for bedside-treatment questions.
8/10
NoveltyThe key novelty is a complete open-source “all-by-all” RWE framework rather than a new estimator alone.
Evidence basis: systematic drug × outcome scope, two-stage SCC/ACNU strategy, centralized architecture. Limiting factor: the paper acknowledges other all-by-all repurposing efforts and builds on established OHDSI methods. Would rise: with head-to-head evidence that REWARD finds higher-value candidates than alternatives. Would fall: if the implementation proves mostly packaging of existing components.
7/10
Method strengthStrong for a screening framework: calibrated observational designs, LSPS, overlap/balance gates, replication, and explicit bias discussion.
Evidence basis: SCC + ACNU, negative controls, standardized mean difference ≤0.10, termination on poor overlap/balance, calibrated inference. Limiting factor: SCC bias, selective/manual ACNU comparator choice, and no all-by-all higher-rigor design. Would rise: automated validated comparator selection, scalable ACNU, prespecified multiplicity strategy, external methodological benchmarking. Would fall: poor negative-control validity or unstable calibration.
6/10
Evidence strengthThe paper supports feasibility and scale better than it supports causal efficacy of generated hypotheses.
Evidence basis: real implementation metrics, prior worked disease/exposure examples, dashboard-level calibrated estimates. Limiting factor: the manuscript is not a prospective validation study and mainly summarizes prior signals. Would rise: prospective replication, clinical-trial enrichment success, or blinded external validation of signal prioritization. Would fall: failure of prioritized associations in pair-specific follow-up.
6/10
External validityOMOP portability is a major strength, but empirical demonstration is concentrated in claims sources.
Evidence basis: six databases spanning five US claims sources and one Japanese claims source; standardized vocabularies. Limiting factor: limited demonstration in EHR-rich, non-claims, or broader international data; claims coding and healthcare-system differences remain. Would rise: replication across independent OMOP networks, EHRs, registries, and additional countries. Would fall: substantial source-specific heterogeneity or cohort-definition instability.
9/10
Implementation valueThe article provides an unusually concrete blueprint: vocabularies, design roles, filtering, architecture, compute environment, storage, dashboard, and open-source package location.
Evidence basis: R/HADES/Java stack, PostgreSQL, CSV intermediates, Azure/Databricks example, 98-GB output, UI filters. Limiting factor: the external repository and code were not independently audited in this appraisal. Would rise: reproducible deployment benchmarks and formal code-quality/validation artifacts. Would fall: if implementation depends heavily on unpublished institutional configuration.

Principal strengths

  • Separation of screening from refinement: computational scale is not conflated with causal rigor.
  • Systematic bias treatment: empirical calibration is central rather than an afterthought, and Figure 5 demonstrates its practical impact.
  • Standardized data boundary: OMOP/RxNorm/SNOMED/ATC make the conceptual system portable across mapped sources.
  • Explicit failure gates: ACNU analyses stop when propensity-score overlap or covariate balance is inadequate.
  • Transparent limitations: authors directly acknowledge protopathic bias, time-varying confounding, unmeasured confounding, comparator-selection burden, and need for manual review.
  • Operational detail: architecture, data flow, compute, storage, filtering, and dashboard functions are described well enough to inform a similar implementation.

Principal limitations and safety concerns

  • Hypothesis generation is not hypothesis testing: the framework can prioritize false positives at enormous scale; clinical action requires independent confirmation.
  • Multiplicity remains challenging: the described default filter uses nominal P<.05 plus effect-size and cross-database replication criteria. Negative-control calibration and replication reduce systematic error, but the manuscript does not describe a conventional familywise/FDR correction for billions of screened pairs.
  • SCC indication/protopathic bias: a drug started because of a condition related to the outcome can create spurious before/after patterns; manual curation is therefore not optional.
  • ACNU is selective and comparator-dependent: the stronger design cannot currently be scaled to the full universe, and comparator selection itself is a scientific decision.
  • Claims-heavy evidence base: diagnoses, exposure duration, and temporality are inferred from administrative data; the paper does not demonstrate equivalent performance in richer clinical datasets.
  • Human review reproducibility: clinical plausibility review is essential but can introduce expert-dependent decisions unless review criteria and adjudication are standardized.
  • Conflict-of-interest context: all authors are employees and stockholders of the pharmaceutical sponsor organization. This does not invalidate the methods, but it increases the importance of independent external replication.

Internal consistency / documentation notes

  • The expansion of the REWARD acronym is not fully consistent within the manuscript: the abstract uses “REal-World Evidence and Research of Drug performance,” the Background uses “REal-World Assessment and Research of Drugs,” and Table 1 gives another abbreviated expansion. This is editorial rather than methodological, but versioned naming should be normalized in downstream documentation.
  • Figure 4’s right branch is labeled ≥1,000 patients, while its caption says “>100 (right).” The branch values align with ≥1,000 and should be treated as the intended threshold.
  • The Results narrative reports nearly 7 billion potential pairs after counting three outcome variants, whereas Figure 4’s raw vocabulary multiplication is ~2.33 billion. The manuscript does not explicitly reconcile these bases; the most plausible interpretation is that the figure omits the three outcome variants.
Bottom line. REWARD is methodologically credible as a discovery infrastructure and is unusually useful as an implementation reference. Its most important design choice is epistemic: it labels broad SCC outputs as signals, reserves stronger ACNU designs for refinement, calibrates against negative controls, requires replication/manual review, and still directs investigators toward pair-specific follow-up. The paper should increase confidence in the feasibility of the pipeline, not confidence that any particular generated drug-benefit association is clinically true.

Confidence in appraisal: high for the manuscript’s content, figures, methods, and stated implementation because the full 12-page source and all main-text visuals were reviewed. Confidence is moderate for claims about runtime reproducibility and software quality because the external GitHub repository and underlying licensed data were not independently inspected.

Implementation / practice takeaways

1. Treat discovery and causal refinement as separate servicesUse a scalable screen to generate candidates, then route selected pairs into a higher-rigor active-comparator design. Do not let one large pipeline pretend that every pair receives the same causal scrutiny.
2. Make negative controls and calibration first-class outputsStore both raw and calibrated estimates, control distributions, and calibration diagnostics. Figure 5 shows why this is not cosmetic: inference can change after calibration.
3. Encode sufficiency/failure gatesFor ACNU, insufficient overlap or residual covariate imbalance should return an explicit non-result rather than forcing an effect estimate.
4. Standardize cohort definitions and version themRxNorm/SNOMED/ATC/OMOP enable scale, but outcome variants, exposure gaps, custom cohorts, and filtering thresholds must be versioned because small definitional changes multiply across billions of models.
5. Keep clinical curation downstream of statistical screeningProtopathic and indication-related artifacts cannot be solved by ranking alone. Manual review should have documented criteria, provenance, and adjudication rather than informal “biologic plausibility” only.
6. Preserve cross-database evidence separately from the meta-analysisThe dashboard pattern is strong: show source-specific estimates, heterogeneity, raw/calibrated results, and pooled estimates so reviewers can identify source-specific contradictions.
7. Use the framework to prioritize follow-up, not prescribeThe appropriate next step for a compelling pair is a tailored observational design, prospective/clinical study, or triangulation with orthogonal evidence such as omics—not direct clinical adoption.
8. Plan infrastructure around data movement and result volumeThe reported SCC output alone was 98 GB. A production implementation needs explicit storage, query, privacy-review, reproducibility, and dashboard strategy—not only statistical code.
